column6: Red flag

column5: Run static analysis and review auth, payment and data-export paths for exploitable flaws.
column6: Any critical finding on an internet-facing endpoint with no fix date.

column5: Count high-severity findings and check whether the same class repeats across endpoints.
column6: The same vulnerability pattern in many places, which points to a process gap, not one bug.

column5: Search for eval/exec, shell commands built from user input and template injection.
column6: User input reaching a shell, eval() or a template engine without validation.

column5: Look for queries built with string formatting instead of parameters or an ORM.
column6: f-strings or string concatenation inside SQL, especially in DELETE/UPDATE.

column5: Check pickle, unsafe YAML loading and similar on data that crosses a trust boundary.
column6: pickle.loads or yaml.load on request bodies, files or queue messages.

column4: Authentication and access control hold up
column5: Review session handling, role checks and tenant isolation on multi-tenant data.
column6: Endpoints that change data without an auth check, or IDs that let one customer read another's records.

column5: Run a rule-based scanner (e.g. Semgrep) against the codebase and triage the results.
column6: Hundreds of open scanner findings nobody has looked at.

column4: No hardcoded secrets in the repository
column5: Scan the code and the full git history for keys, tokens and passwords.
column6: Live credentials in the repo; past staff and contractors still have them.

column5: Look for service-account JSON, TLS and signing keys in the tree.
column6: A *.json or *.pem key file in source control.

column4: No cloud or payment provider tokens
column5: Check specifically for AWS, Stripe, GitHub and Slack tokens.
column6: A live Stripe or AWS key: direct access to money or infrastructure.

column5: Look for passwords and API keys set as string literals or defaults.
column6: os.getenv('KEY', 'real-secret-value') style fallbacks.

column5: Check for .env, .env.prod and similar files in the repository.
column6: .env files with production database URLs or keys in git.

column4: Debug and auto-reload disabled in production
column5: Confirm debug flags and dev servers are off in production config.
column6: Stack traces or debug pages reachable on the live site.

column5: Review ORM/engine settings: SQL echo, SSL, pool limits.
column6: SQL logging of real customer data, or unencrypted connections.

column5: Run npm audit / pip-audit (or an SBOM scan) against the lockfiles.
column6: Critical advisories in packages that are directly reachable from the internet.

column5: List high advisories by package and whether a patched version exists.
column6: Many high advisories with available fixes that were never applied.

column5: Count moderate advisories and the age of the oldest unpatched one.
column6: A long backlog of old advisories: dependencies aren't being maintained.

column5: Find GPL/AGPL packages in a proprietary product, including transitive ones.
column6: AGPL code in a SaaS product: may oblige publishing your own source.

column5: Flag LGPL/MPL packages and how they are linked or modified.
column6: Modified LGPL/MPL code shipped without meeting its obligations.

column5: List packages with missing or non-standard licenses.
column6: Unknown licenses on core packages: unpriced legal risk.

column5: Build the project and run the type checker from a clean checkout.
column6: The main branch doesn't build, or type errors are suppressed wholesale.

column5: Run the project's linters with its own config.
column6: Linting disabled in CI, or thousands of errors left in place.

column5: Review money, permissions and data-integrity code paths for wrong results.
column6: Billing, refund or quota logic with unhandled edge cases.

column5: Measure cyclomatic complexity; list functions above 20.
column6: Core business logic in a handful of 500-line functions.

column5: Check what share of functions are moderately complex.
column6: Complexity spread everywhere: every change is slow and risky.

column5: Look for global state, hidden coupling and copy-pasted rules.
column6: Global mutable state shared across requests.

column5: Detect duplicated blocks across the repository.
column6: The same business rule implemented differently in several places.

column5: Find files nothing imports and that aren't entry points.
column6: Large amounts of dead code that inflate the codebase you are paying for.

column5: Check that layering, data access and error handling follow one pattern.
column6: Three different ways to call the database, each with its own bugs.

column5: List competing conventions (config, logging, auth checks).
column6: Every service or module invented its own conventions.

column5: Build the import graph and look for cycles.
column6: Modules that can't be changed or extracted independently.

column5: Find modules that import many internal modules.
column6: A 'utils' or 'core' module every change has to touch.

column5: Review service boundaries, schema design and single points of failure.
column6: A design that needs a rewrite to reach the projected scale.

column5: Look for N+1 queries, blocking I/O in async code and unbounded queries.
column6: Costs or latency that grow faster than usage.

column4: At least one test file per five source files
column5: Compare test files to source files, and look at what the tests cover.
column6: Almost no tests around payments, auth or data integrity.

column5: Check for coverage tooling and reports.
column6: Nobody knows which parts of the product are unprotected.

column5: List top-level modules with no tests at all.
column6: Whole services or apps with zero tests.

column4: CI runs the tests on every change
column5: Check the pipeline runs tests and blocks merges on failure.
column6: CI exists but doesn't run tests, or failures are ignored.

column4: No one wrote half or more of the code
column5: Look at the commit share per contributor over the repo's history.
column6: One engineer authored most of the commits: a bus factor of one.

column5: Count contributors with 10% or more of commits.
column6: Only one or two people understand the core systems.

column5: Check when the codebase was last changed.
column6: No commits for months: nobody may be left who can maintain it.

column4: The main author is still active
column5: Check the top contributor's most recent commit.
column6: The person who wrote most of the code has stopped committing.

column4: Two or more people actively committing
column5: Count contributors active in the last 90 days.
column6: A single active maintainer for every post-close fix.
